utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. I should say before we start that on Wednesday, that's Wednesday the 4th, we'll be stopping at 1.15 p.m. in order to allow another Trial Chamber to give its sentencing judgement in a case. So please bear that in mind, we'll stop at 1.15 on Wednesday. Now, this is Captain Hansen; and in accordance the procedure that I had explained, I'll allow both parties to put questions whether by way of cross-examination or examination to Captain Hansen, and these will be based on the statement that has been provided. So let us start with Mr. Whiting of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Captain Hansen.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My name is Alex Whiting, and I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case. We've never met before, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And we have never spoke before, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I arrived in The Hague on Friday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please bear in mind that they are being interpreted, so please make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just repeat that. You have to observe a pause between the question and answer in the interest of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and thank you to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Captain Hansen, I'm going ask if you could -- we have a very short time, so if could you try to make your answers as brief as possible, even if yes or no is sufficient, then just limit it, please, to just yes or no. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I want to draw your attention to the 28th of June, 1995. You were in the PTT building when an air bomb hit the TV tower in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I was in the TV building; but if it was an air bomb, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When the bomb hit, were you in the TV building or the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. After it hit, another UNMO came into the PTT building and spoke with you about what he saw; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: He came to make a report about what he had observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You yourself did not see anything; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to show you a report that you have written.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher I would like to pass out copies. I know everybody probably has a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Captain, this is 65 ter 536. Captain, is this your report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: This is my report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in the report, you include a grid reference. Do you see that in the first bullet point?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who came up with that grid reference?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: The UNMO that reported this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the -- your testimony is that the UNMO came into the building and told you this information and gave you a specific grid reference?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. We always worked with a grid references; and when he came in, I asked him to -- to tell me where it was fired from because he had seen where it was fired from. And he went down to the parking place again together with another UNMO, and they came back and reported this was the grid it was fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask that a map be shown - it's 65 ter 3096 - on the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, may I just ask the Captain: How are grid references determined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you said that the UNMO went and returned and gave you the grid reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a technical matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came back and showed on the map and as the bomb was fired from a place very near to where he parked the car, within to 200 to 300 metres from he parked the car. And he could point out the direction, and from that we were quite sure about the grid reference he gave as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm really trying to get at is the numbers 866587, how is that arrived at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I referred to a map we were using by the UNMOs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness's microphone need to be turned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's my microphone that was on. Yes, please give us the answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say that they refer to a map was used by the UNMOs in Sector Sarajevo to the map. Do you want me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What information would they need to have to arrive at the grid reference, this number 866587.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a reading of a map. If you read the grid to find -- find an exact place on the map. I'm not sure about your question, because it's -- it's obvious to me what to use the grid for. Are you asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is some basic empirical data on which the grid reference is determined.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're asking about, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Perhaps I could clarify it with a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Whiting, and we can return to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, Captain Hansen, and correct me if I am wrong, that the first number, 866, refers to a number that you derive on one side of the map, that is the left-hand side of the map on the grid; and the second number then is 587, and you go along the top of the map and where those two points meet is what the grid reference refers to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the grid that is used has a correlation to distance; that is, you can calculate -- if you have one grid reference and then another grid reference, you can calculate the distance between the two points, because they refer to every 100 metres or so?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: In this case, they refer to 100 metres?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this map, you can see there is the PTT building, the TV tower, and the grid reference that has been identified. And you have said that you have identified the grid reference as being a point some 2 to 300 metres away from the PTT parking lot. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at the time this incident occurred -- well, by the way, you mentioned - and I don't believe it is in your report - that the UNMO, who says he saw this, calculated the grid reference with another UNMO. Who -- do you know the identity of this other UNMO?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you don't remember the identity of either of these two UNMOs that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I think I remember one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get back to that. Now, at the time this occurred, the UNPROFOR was using the PTT building as a headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we're going a little quickly, if you could take a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could we slow down a little bit, please, because I'm listening to the translation, and I find it difficult to follow the English. So kindly just slow down a little, please, because the speed is rather great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please slow down a bit in the -- in the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, Captain Hansen, that there were over 100 people, maybe even 150 people, working in the PTT building at the time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: There was a lot more than 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many would you say there were?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I know there was a headquarters for Sector Sarajevo, and there was the people working for the headquarters for the military operation that -- as UNMOs, we were only 80 UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But how many total people would you say were working in that building, since you said it was more 150. You said a lot more than 150.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: It could be between 3 and 500 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that building is building of several floors and it has windows looking in the direction of this grid reference. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. But all the windows on most of them were blended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of anybody else who saw this bomb being launched from this location?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You yourself participated in the investigation of the bomb on the TV tower later that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: We were not allowed to carry out any investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you participated with the Bosnian police later on that day in the investigation. You were present when they did the investigation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're certain about that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what the results of the investigation were?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're not aware that the results of the investigation determined that the bomb that hit the TV tower was a 250-kilo bomb -- air bomb?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: As I have been telling to an investigation team later on in September, I think it was in September, we were not allowed to make any investigation at the scene, and we were -- what was not normal we were not informed by the Bosnian the result of this investigation. They always carried out themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say "we were not informed," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: The UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that the UNMOs were not informed? I mean, you can speak about yourself not being informed but how do you know about others?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Because as being the operation officer, I was the one who always received the reports from the Bosnians whenever they have carried out an investigation. They wanted -- in many cases, they wanted us to -- I'm missing the word. They wanted to us confirm that we made a report that was similar to the one that had been doing. In this case, we were not allowed to carry out any investigation. I was on the scene where the bomb hit, shortly after it hit. But I was waiting there for, I think, two hours, and we were not allowed to carry out any investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were not allowed to carry out an investigation. You were not allowed by whom? Who were the people that prevented you from conducting an investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian police and military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you were on the scene. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: If I can explain how things happen. After this UNMO came to the office and reported, we made the report which was sent to the offices where it was meant to be sent. I went down to the liaison officer from the BiH and told him that we were now going -- the UNMOs, we were now going to the scene. I took one of the UNMOs from the PTT building, one of my UNMOs working together with me. And we arrived to the scene, we were the first UNMOs or the first UN personnel to arrive. We went into where the bomb had hit and were then taken away from -- from the scene of the either police or military, I don't remember that. There was still incoming shells at that moment and, they told us were not allowed to carry out any investigation for our own security. We were then waiting for, as I said before, I believe more than two hours and were not allowed to go no the scene and carry out any investigation. That was, for us, very unusual because normally the BiH wanted us and always pushed us to -- or wanted us to carry out the investigation. But in this case we were not allowed to do, and afterwards we didn't receive any report from the BiH about this, their own investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's take this one step at a time, Captain. I'm going to ask if we could look --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: First, could we admit this map into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it. Give it a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes P517.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we now look at Prosecution Exhibit 134, please, and if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Captain, this is a report from the Bosnian police about the air bomb investigation -- about the investigation into the air bomb that hit the TV tower that day. And if you look at the bottom there, it says: "UN military observes, group SW-2, Captain Idriz from Kenya and Captain Thomas from Denmark and others were present in the investigation." Now, I take it that the "Captain Thomas from Denmark" is a reference to you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And according to this report, you were present along with the others for the investigation. Are you now saying that is not true?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I am saying I was not present at any investigation. I was there waiting for two hours, and I had to leave, again, without carrying out any investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that the air bomb hit at approximately 9.20, 9.22 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see that according to this report in the second paragraph the -- this police centre was informed at 10.45 and then proceeded to the scene.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you were there for some two-hours, you would have been there when they were there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you said you did not participate in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I was taken to another room. When I arrived to the TV building, I went to the scene where the impact had been, immediately, and then I was taken away to another room. And we were waiting in another room for two-hours, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you a short video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please explain what you need by taken to another room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told that because for my own security or our security because there is still incoming shells, at the moment, we were taken to another room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you free to leave the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was free to leave the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you remained in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was two hours. It's a long time ago so it's difficult to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And who else was in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When reading the report now, I believe it was Captain Idriz from Kenya.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who is that Captain Idriz? Is that the same UNMO who gave you the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that, yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Captain Hansen, when you say you were taken to the scene, does that mean down at the place where the bomb had exploded on the ground, or were you also able to visit the roof of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at the bottom of the building where there was damages from the bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But you were not on the top of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Captain, I'm going to show you a very brief, one-minute video clip of an air bomb being launched, and I will ask you questions about it afterwards. Bear in mind that this clip, this air bomb that is being launched is an 100-kilogram air bomb, as opposed to the 250-kilogram --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before watching this video, this video was disclosed to the Defence, but if the Prosecutor could tell us what time the launch of this air bomb refers to, because I don't believe this is relevant in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, give us some more information about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The -- it's the air bomb that -- the launching of the air bomb in the video is -- I can't say when it is. It's during the war, but that's not the issue that I'm showing it for. And our expert, Mr. Zecivic, will talk about this video clip and talk about the launching of the air bomb and identify what it is and so forth. There will be further evidence about it later, but I'm showing it foro different purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To show what it looks like and ask him whether such a thing would be visible and how -- and to what area it -- if it were launched from the location that we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, just explain the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- the witness has testified that this information that he received is that it was launched some 2 or 300 metres away from the parking lot. I would like to show a launch and have him explain whether that would -- how visible that would be from that location, whether it would be unusual to have seen it, or whether other people would have seen it. So it is directly relevant because he has talked about launch from that location. We want to show what it looks like and how visible it would. It seems to me that is absolutely on point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. No. He knows the location. He was at the location, and he knows how far it was. He has testified how far it was, and he knows how visible that location would be from that distance and he knows the area. So it's -- it goes directly to how visible this would and whether others would see this. And I don't see any -- I certainly don't see any prejudice in showing it. If ultimately Your Honours conclude it's not relevant, that's fine. But it seems me there is a sufficient basis to show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The difficulty we have, Mr. Prosecutor, is that as interesting as this might be, and I would certainly like to see the video, the video has nothing to do with this witness. He didn't see it. He has no idea where it could have come from. He didn't see the launch. He didn't see the trajectory. The only thing he saw was that he had a short glimpse of the impact. That is why I have difficulties in accepting that in relation this witness this video is admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has been called because he has information about somebody else who saw it. He was there at the time. He knows the location that was identified as the launch point, and he can testify whether -- whether, in his view, a lot of people in the area would have seen this launch as it is depicted or whether it was not unusual that only one person to his knowledge saw it. So even though he himself did not see it, he was there. He is familiar with the area, and he has talked about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But has he ever seen an air bomb in passage, in flight?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. The question is going to be -- It's not the trajectory; it's the launch. The question is going to be would this have been visible -- this launch have been visible from that location, from the PTT building or other areas. Would -- given what he shows about the time and where it was launched from and who was around, would he -- would others have seen it. It's -- it seems to me impossible to bring a witness who is going to testify about somebody having seen something and not test, be able it test whether that was surprising that to his knowledge only one person saw it. It's foreclosing my ability to test this evidence. And again, I don't -- there is no certainly prejudice. At worst, we're going to end up with evidence that you have ultimately deem is not relevant. But I don't think -- it will take about two minutes to do this. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that this raises another issue, because all the evidence which are introduced before -- all the evidence which is introduced before your Chamber will help you to determine which kind of device hit the television building on that day in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I think that this is going a little bit too fast, and this is not relevant to our case. And I think it would be wise to ask the expert who is going be called to testify to spell this out in detail for us. But here we have a fact witness who is testifying about something which is quite specific, and to my mind this video has nothing to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just respond to that. There is also evidence in the case that this -- the bomb hit was an air bomb, and it was a 250-kilogram air bomb. So there is certainly a basis for putting this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber's ruling is that the video is not to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at 65 ter exhibit 3094.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Captain, do you recognise this photograph to be a view from the PTT building parking lot, in fact, it's from the upper parking lot?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: It is. It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise what is in the red square to be what was known as OP4.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recognise that in the yellow box is roughly the area where, according to the information that you say you received, the -- this air bomb was launched from?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you accept, sir, that a launching of a missile or an air bomb from that location would be highly visible.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: It would be visible from the area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, do you accept the possibility that the UNMO that you spoke to made a mistake and did not see the air bomb launched from that location but saw it fly over that location? Would you accept that possibility, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: There is always a possibility. But from what he told me at the moment and from going down to the place where he saw it, where he parked the car, the car was parked closer to the wall that you see at the middle of the picture. So when he went out from the car, he could easily look into the area. Sorry. I also believe that the new building that you see at the right of the picture is a new one that has been built after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just for the record, that building is -- the building just all the way to the right, it's grey, red, and blue. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you ever seen an air bomb being launched?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I have not seen the launch of it, but I have seen it when it is flying in the air. But the report doesn't tell anything about -- or my report doesn't tell anything about an air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. I'm just going that you accept for a moment - I understand that you yourself do not know what kind of a projectile it was - but it is, to be fair, a rapid and unexpected event. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Say again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When an air bomb is launched, or let's say any bomb is launched, -- no, let me put this differently. The UNMO who provided you this information did not know in advance that this bomb was going to be launched; correct.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. He reported to me that he parked the car with the front pointing -- front of the car pointing in direction where you have the yellow figure on the -- on the picture. When he was standing out and went to close his door, the door of the car, he saw it launched. And attached to the report you have filed here, there was also a sketch where he tried to draw a sketch from the projectile that was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if he had ever seen an air bomb being launched before?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so I come back to my question: Since he didn't know it was going to happen, it is a sudden unexpected event, he had never seen it before, isn't it possible that he made a mistake when he said where it was launched from and that in fact it just flew over that location?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: There might always be a possibility that he makes mistake. As UNMOs, we were supposed to report only what we had seen with our own eyes; and if you look at all the reports that we had filed by UNMOs, from the when I was an operation officer, I very often refused to report things that people believe that had seen. But this UNMO came to me and he was quite sure about what he had seen. We questioned him several times from different angles to see if there should be any mistakes about it, because he as well knew that this was an important witness he had -- thing he been seeing. He was a Muslim UNMO himself, so he knew that it could have important to -- it could be important and it could have -- an effect on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, you say that as UNMOs, you're trained to report what we had seen with our own eyes, and you say this was important information. But the UNMO who says he saw it did not in fact report it, did he?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: He reported it himself, but he was not supposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. I'm going to interrupt you there for a moment, sir. He did not write a report about this, did he?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: The UNMOs were not supposed to write reports like this. They were supposed to bring information in for the UNMO headquarters, and I'm an -- as an UNMO operation officer, I was supposed to write the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it the case that he did not want to write the report because he thought it was sensitive, and you offered to write the report for him. Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So he ordinarily would have written a report about something like that but chose not to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No. If he had been in his UNMO team, he could have been writing a report that would have been sent into the UNMO headquarters and then I would send the report for the headquarters in Zagreb and for the headquarters in Bosnia. But always it would be me or one of my operation officers who would write the report and not him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is not very clear, because earlier you were asked whether -- the UNMO did not want to write the report because he thought it was sensitive and that you offered to write the report for him. And you said that that was correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. If he had been in the UNMO team, he would have been writing -- if he had been out in the team in the building itself, he would have been writing a report, sending it in for the UNMO headquarters, and then I would have been writing the final report that would have been send to the headquarters for the UNMO in Zagreb. In this case, when he came directly the parking place, he had something to do in the building; and when parking the car, he saw this missile rocket that was launched, so he came directly to my office. And when we were discussing about this, he could have been writing the report his own hand, but I still would have been the one to write the report to send to Zagreb. And that is the report that you see in front of me -- or in front of you. Attached to the report, there is a sketch which he had been doing himself and this was made by his hand and not by mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Captain, I believe the difficulty we have in fully appreciating your testimony is that it is unclear to us why the UNMO simply did not write a report. Under normal circumstances, he would have been obliged to do so, wouldn't he? But I understand that you are saying that he was not in case because he was not a member of any team that had business to do in that area? Or how are we to understand your explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry that I am unclear. He was a member of a team coming into the PTT building where the headquarters was. When he had been out in the team -- if he had been out in a team or if he had returned to the team, then he was supposed to write a report that should have been sent in to headquarters, where I was sitting as an operation officer, and then I would be rewriting his report, what we did all the time. The report we were sending for the headquarters in Zagreb, they were sent by CapSat and not in a written form in a report like you see it on paper here. So they were always been done by the operation officers, and I was the operation officer in charge of the operation officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you say out in the team, do you mean that were he out in the field.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was normally out in the team. As you see, if you take a look of the picture within the red square, that is one of the teams that was placed on the inside of the Sector Sarajevo, on the BiH side. And this UNMO was placed in one of those teams. If he hadn't had anything to do in the PTT building, he would have returned to the team; and together with the team leader, he would have been writing a report that would have been sent in for the headquarters, the headquarters for UNMO Sector Sarajevo; then I would have been writing the same report again and sent it to the headquarters Zagreb. Now, when he was in the PTT building, instead of sitting down that he was writing a report, he was telling me; and if you look at the sketch he has been doing, I have been using the same words as he has been using in the sketch himself. So this is the sketch and report he has been doing himself, and I was the one to send the Sector Sarajevo report to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's because he was in the PTT building --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he came in the PTT, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- why he wasn't required to write a report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Captain, I'm going to have to press this issue a bit more, because now I think you given two different explanations for why he did not write a report. You said, on the one hand, he did not write a report because it was too sensitive, and he did not want to write a report, suggesting that ordinarily he would have been required to write a report. And now, on the other hand, you're suggesting it was simply because he was in the PTT building, and it was a matter of convenience. Which of these explanations is correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: You can say that both them are correct, because he didn't want to put his name in the report. We normally didn't put names in reports. As you see, before there -- when teams were making investigations, they were always put a name on the investigations, who carried out the investigation. In this case, we decided not to put his name on --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, now, the report -- you did not sit there in the PTT building and write this report, did you? You didn't write the report until the next day.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, look at the date on the report.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The date on the report is the 29th of June at 12.30 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: And then there would be another report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, this report that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You wrote the following day, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So you -- when you say he came into the PTT building and you could just write the report, you did not write the report that day.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: But there was then another report written the same day for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If there was a report written on the 28th of June, why would you have to write this report the following day with the exact same information in it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Because there was a daily report that was sent every day before 1800 in the evening, and then an update of the daily report every day at 2400 hours. And this one, as it is written, the subject is "Special report under impact on the TV building," but there would be -- in the files there would be a report on what has happened as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Captain, are you sure about this information or are you just kind of --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Just to clarify, so there is in existence on the file, a report which is part of the daily reports for the 28th on this incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There would will be, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This special report makes no reference to that. It does not say it is an update or that this information has already been provided, does it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Because that was not supposed to be like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't -- if somebody is reading this report, wouldn't you want to indicate that this information has already been the subject of a previous report? Wouldn't that be important?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: It wasn't done that way, and I think that at that time people understood what we had been reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you say that you chose not to include the name of the UNMO. Isn't that important information that should be included in the report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, why not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Because as reporting, as an UNMO, it's not a question of the name of the UNMO, but it's a report from an UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, just a few minutes ago, you told us how you were trained as UNMOs that were trained to report what had you seen, that this was important information. How is it possible that it would not important who saw it. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Because at the time we knew the UNMO who he was, and it's still possible to find him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, isn't that, in fact, not clear since you couldn't remember and you are still not certain who the UNMO is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And isn't it true that you chose not to put his name in. Ordinarily you would put his name in, but you chose not to in this case. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. But it's not ordinary to put a name in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from the report that you now say you wrote on the 28th of June, did you tell any body on the 28th of June that you had gotten this information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: It was not a secret to anyone because the UNMO came into the operation room --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I want to interrupt for a moment. Please, focus on my question. Did you tell anyone on the 28th of June, putting aside the report you now say that you wrote, did you tell anybody on the 28th of June about this information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that we did not tell anyone about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's look for a few moments at the report, and I'm going to -- do you know anything about air bombs.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Not specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Do you -- are I aware -- you give the dimensions that the UNMO claims the bomb was. Are you aware that a -- that a 250-kilogram air bomb is approximately one and a half times wider and three times longer than those dimensions? Is that something that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I have seen that the air bombs, the other ones passing the PTT building, I have seen them flying in the air, and I have seen the impact of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so you are aware of this a 250-kilogram air bomb is much larger than the dimensions that are provided in this report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I think so, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that when an air bomb is launched, there is a smoke trail from the rockets and that the smoke trail stops when the rockets run out of fuel, and then the air bomb descends and lands on its target?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you say here that the UNMO observed no smoke. There was no smoke observed while Selos [phoen] trajectory object was in flight. Based on your experience, wouldn't that indicate to that you the rockets had run out of fuel already when the UNMO saw it, and it was already heading toward its target?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: The UNMO didn't report about an bomb. He reported about a missile or a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Accept for a moment that it's an air bomb. If it were an air bomb - accept that for a moment - then wouldn't this information, based on your experience, suggest that the -- that the air bomb had already -- the fuel from the rockets had already run out, and it was heading -- it is descending toward its target?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I'm not supposed as an UNMO, I think now, to -- to think about if it as an air bomb or significant. I was at the time only supposed to report what the UNMOs reported to me, and that's what I'm do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm asking you not as an UNMO; I'm asking you as a witness to this event and based on the information that you received and your understanding of how these worked. Accept that it ask an air bomb, then the information that you received would suggest that the rockets had already run out of fuel at the time he saw it, since did he not see any smoke. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about why you're asking. I mean, if it's an air bomb, or a rocket that has been run out of fuel, then of course there would be no smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You say on page 2 of your report that -- it's the second-to-last paragraph. You say that the UNMO team at OP4 was taking shelter at the time. It did not see anything. That is not true, is it? That information is not true?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: If I have been writing it here, then I believe it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: From the OP4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who in OP4?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: The people present at OP4. We, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us a name?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No, I can't tell any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, sir, isn't it true, that -- were you familiar with Mr. Brennskag, Per Brennskag?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I remember his name, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know that, in fact, he was at OP4 on that day, and he observed this very air bomb?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure. Because when I had within writing it here, then I have reason to believe that we have contacted OP4 and questioned them about if they had observed anything, because they should have been able to see down in the area as you point out yourself. So when I have been writing it here, then I have only reason to believe that they didn't see anything at the movement when it was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you can't tell us who you talked to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you talk to that person?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Right after when we did the investigation and before filing the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You agree with me, don't you, that from OP4 you could see this location perfectly?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just ask, Captain, in your report, you say that OP4 was taking cover in the shelter at that time because of shelling at the time of the incident. How did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I got by radio contact to the team, by calling them in. I don't remember at the moment, but I am sure I would never have been writing anything in the report if it was not a fact. So -- to make the investigation -- to finish the investigation, it was important for us to clarify if anyone else had seen something similar. And as I write in the report, a FreBat soldier -- the UNMO reported to us that a FreBat soldier was close to him in the parking lot. We were not able to find him and, therefore, didn't get in the further information from him. So I don't remember this part of the report. But I'm sure now when seeing it that I would never have been writing it without having taking contact with the team in OP4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And was the radio contact made by you personally or by somebody else and then the information passed on to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I say "radio contact," I'm quite sure that we would not have been talking about something like this on radio. So I would have probably called in the team to the OP room and have been talking personally to the people about this case. But I don't remember, so it could have been on radio. So it's most unlikely that we have been making this on radio, so probably it would had been called in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain. When would you have been able to see someone from OP4 in your office? Would that be later that same day, or would it be the day after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would probably have been the same day. I'm quite sure it had been the same day. The reason for, when I'm asked if it's most unlikely that other people, why they hadn't seen it. At the time, there was outgoing shelling from the BiH side and there was a lot of incoming shelling from the -- from the other side. So that was -- that was the reason for people, of course, to take cover in shelters and could have been the reason why there wasn't any other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the information from OP4 was in fact the air bomb had been observed, the air bomb that hit the TV tower had been observed that day, would you accept that your report could be inaccurate, could be mistaken?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember that part of it, as I told earlier. So if could you bring in an UNMO that now can tell that he has been observing at the time, it would be most -- I would be very surprised about that, because I'm sure about all the reports I have been writing from the mission that I would never been writing anything without being 100 per cent sure. That is what I was teaching the UNMOs, that we should never report anything that we were not 100 per cent sure about. So when writing that they were in shelter, I'm sure that someone from OP4 had been reporting to me that they were in shelter at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But none of that information is included in the report, is it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: What? What --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: None of the information about how you spoke to, when you spoke to, how you spoke to them, none of that is in the report, is it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That is correct, because we didn't put names in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is there any information that is in this report dated the 29th of June that was not included, that you didn't know on the 28th of June that would have -- in other words, what is new about this report and what is the reason for writing it, if you knew all of this information on the 28th of June?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I have no idea why it's written on the 29th. It's probably because I have been questioned to write a new report about this, because I knew that this information was sent on the -- as I remember the situation, when I reported this, I sent it by secure means by CapSat. It was sent to Sector Sarajevo, the headquarter for the whole UN troops. It was sent for the headquarter for the Bosnia UN, and it was sent for UN Zagreb. About 20 minutes after I sent this report, I was called on telephone and I was told to forget about this report. I was told that I couldn't forget it because I had sent it already by secure means to the three officers that I was supposed to send it. And after another 20 minutes, I was then called again and was told that I should just forget about this report and everything has been settled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you going to follow this up, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was going to, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you just remember this, what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this something that you just remembered?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No, have I remembered it all the time since it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Twenty minutes after you sent the report on the 29th of June or the report on the 28th of June?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I'm quite sure it was on the 28th I was told not to do anything more about this and not to -- to give the information to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, were you interviewed by an ICTY investigator in this case, if I can find your interview, on the 8th or 9th of September -- the 8th and 9th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you say anything about what you have just told us about being told 20 minutes after you sent the report to forget about the report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please speak a little by the closer to the microphone because we can't here you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 3087, please, and if we could look at --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, it's D72. This is Exhibit D72. It's already been given a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you don't have it in front of you -- or you might, you might. I'm not sure if I have it or not, but it's on the screen now. And if you could look at page 3 there, in the middle of the page, it says: "I investigated among all the other shellings also an impact on the TV building." Now, first of all, you told us earlier that you had not investigated it.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So why did you say in this statement that you did investigate it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I might have been using the wrong words about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in the next paragraph, you say: "At that time, we could not find any fragments or parts of the projectile that hit the building." So that indicates that you participated in the investigation or were aware of it, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I have to see. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It doesn't say anything -- you speak about the UNMO, but it didn't say anything about this information that you have now provided today, that you were told 20 minutes -- it doesn't say anything about being told 20 minutes after filing a report to forget about this. There is nothing about that in here, is there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I was not asked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, don't you think that was important information? If you were told 20 minutes after writing a report to forget about it, don't you think that was something important that should have been told?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I was still in the UN mission so I didn't think about it as important information for those investigations at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In your recent conversations with Barry Hogan, the investigator from the OTP, you also did not mention this information, did you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I was not asked about it, and I didn't see it as important information for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Captain, are you just making up answers as you go along here today?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, as a series of reports, and I think you probably have them in front of you, but I have copies. It's R 0025651 to 5663, and this is 65 ter 3088.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Captain, you have had an opportunity to read over these reports, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do they accurately set out the details of the conflict that you had with the ABiH liaison office on that day?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: It does, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you turn to the page that is marked -- has the last four digits 5654 on the top. It's dated the 28th of June, 1995. It's a patrol report. Was that report written by you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's written by me, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look, sort of -- the sixth paragraph you say, it starts off: "When I came back from the investigation." Doesn't that again suggest that you were present or involved in the investigation in the TV tower?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: It says that I came back from a patrol that was supposed to be an investigation. We called everything as we drove out as either an observation or an investigation And I was supposed to go out for an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Captain, is it fair to say that when after you received the information from the UNMO, you went to the ABiH liaison office and is it fair to say that Captain Nermin there believed that you said that the ABiH had fired the air bomb or fired the bomb on the TV tower that's what he thought you said, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's right .

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you deny saying that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes. And I still recall what I said when I went to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, in fact, when you went to his office that is exactly what you believed that is correct the ABiH had fired the bomb, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes. But I have been learned myself and thought the other UNMOs to be impartial, so when I went to the office and asked them to stop firing for one hour. That has happened very often in the past that we succeeded in that. I asked him to stop the fire and he said that we should ask the -- the Serbian side, the Bosnian Serb side to stop the firing. And I said, "You were firing from both side, and you will have to stop the fire or we will ask to you stop the fire." And in this case with the TV building, he misunderstood me when going down there and he asked me if I believed that there had been firing themselves. And I said I have no reason to believe anything before we have carried the out the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So let me just get it clear here. You went in there believing that the ABiH had fired the bomb. He believes that that is what you said, but you still deny that you said anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I didn't use that -- I didn't use those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in your report here that you wrote on the 28th of June, 1995, there's no mention of this unnamed UNMO and what he reported to you, is there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could these documents be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just have a couple of more questions. Sir, are you aware -- oh I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just to be clear, this is 65 ter, 03088. This will be Exhibit P519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just before you leave that issue, would you tell us, Captain, who was it that told you 20 minutes after you wrote the report that you should forget about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember his name or rank or function. But I was called from someone in the headquarters for the UNMOs in Zagreb, the overall headquarters for the UNMOs, that I should forget about this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told this person that I, of course, couldn't forget about the report because it was already sent to three different offices; and then after another 20 minutes - I remember it as 20 minutes - but a short period, I was called again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: By the same person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was the same person, and I have no reason not to believe it. And, of course, I knew the person, so I knew when he was calling me that, that was what I had to do. It was an order and, as I said, after another 20 minutes, I was called again and said that the case has been settled, and we should just forget about this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The person calling you, you say you don't remember his name, but what about his rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was for sure been a superior to me in the way that maybe not in rank, because when working as an UNMO the rank doesn't matter. You can have a high function as a captain or you can have a high rank and has a -- be working as a team member. So, he was for sure one of my superiors or one of those people working in headquarters to whom I have to -- to listen to when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you -- you understood this to be an order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that to be an order, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks, Captain. Now, this took place -- the two phone calls that you did receive from Zagreb, they took place on the 28th of June, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quite sure it was on the 28th, because it was a short time after all this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now the day after, on the 29th, you did proceed to file a report. That was the report that we saw just a while ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that was a detailed report but it has to be in the report on the 28th as well. You -- if you find my reports on the 28th or from the OP room, from Sector Sarajevo, you will for sure find details as well about this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. We did have -- we do have your report of the 28th of June, and we also have seen your report from the following day on the 29th. And my question is: If you were told to forget about the whole thing on the 28th, then why didn't you just forget about the whole thing? I mean, the difficulty I have is that did you not forget about the whole thing. You actually did proceed, and on the following day you did file your final report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a long time ago, so I might forget the timings of this. So when I received this order about forgetting it, it might have been after reporting this special report. But what I'm saying is that there would for sure would be details about the incident in the report from the 28th. So it might have been that the timing of this. What has happened is that I was ordered to forget about the case on the 29th; but as all those things happened, things they happened very fast. I'm quite sure that there must be a report, a similar report like this on the 28th that has been filed; and after that report, I have been told to forget about it. Because on the 29th, for me it would have been too late. I still remember when all this happened, the rumours about the incident run around in PTT building, the headquarters, Sector Sarajevo. It was running around; and a short time after the incident, people came to the office and asked if this was correct that an UNMO had seen a projectile fired from the BiH side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to clarify, we do have both of your reports; the one from the 28th and also the one from the 29th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And it's in our files. So what you're saying now is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really hate to interrupt, but I'm not sure that the report from the 28th is the type of report that he is referring to. I think the report from the 28th pertains to a specific matter and is not a daily situation report or a daily report. I'm not aware that we have the report from the 28th that he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this clarifies one of the matters. May I just have one last question put to you, Captain Hansen, and that is that on the reports, your special report. You say that an UNMO coming into the PTT building, parking his car on the lower parking place observed the following. My question relates to the word "the lower parking place," because from the picture that we saw just a while ago, I think it was Exhibit P518, it seemed to me that that picture was taken from the top of the parking place --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- where obviously your view would have been much better than had you parked your car on the lower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm sure when writing the report I have to stick to the report that I have been writing; and when we at the time had been writing on the lower parking place, then for sure he has been coming into the lower parking place and parked his car there. Now, when the Prosecutor showed me the picture from the -- the upper parking place, that was then was what was in my mind. But by reading the report, I'm 100 percent sure that the UNMO has been coming into the lower parking place, and that is the place from where he has seen the projectile being fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But can I just ask you again: You said that you went with him back to the parking place --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- for him to show you what he had seen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And do you remember whether, when you went with him --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- did you go to the lower parking place or the top one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to his car because his car was still parked outside. He came into the building, parked his car. For some reason, he had something to do in the building. I don't know if it was to visit me or to do other business in the building. So when he came to report this, we immediately went down to his car to observe from his car, and he could point out from the direction from where this was fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And could you see the presumed origin of fire from the lower parking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see the place he was pointing at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain, please, I have another question, and I'd like to come back to your attitude because I don't understand it from well. What you did after you got from the phone call you got from Zagreb. You said that as an UNMO you were determined to report only on what had you seen yourself and not what on which you had been told about, which is fine. But when you wrote your first report on June 28, one of your superior in Zagreb, that had not seen anything because he was in Zagreb, told you to drop the whole thing, and you want to only do and see what -- only report on what you have seen on the terrain. So on June 29, you rewrote your report maintaining what you had stated the day before. But what is really striking here is when the ICTY investigators interviewed you on June 8 and 9, a few months later, you do not mention this phone call from Zagreb, which I believe is totally contrary to what an UNMO should do, because normally an UNMO in his conscience should report what he had seen. So how can you explain the fact that you had been so silent about this phone call up until now? Is it because you were afraid of your superiors, or because you believe that your report was wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no reason to believe that my report is wrong. When I say that UNMOs are to report what they see and the facts they see, it is also means that when you are the operation officer, you have to believe notice UNMOs that is working as UNMOs. So whatever they report to you, you'll have to write and believe in it. About not telling about those phone calls to the investigators, that was not a question that was coming up when they questioned me and I was still working in the UN mission, so I was not thinking about to report it or to inform them about those phone calls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it -- did it happen often that a superior would ask you to modify reports that had been the written by you, taking into account what you had seen on the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this incident with your superior, that was something really serious. Don't you think that you should have notified it to the authorities to make sure that the UN was running properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still remember the situation, and I was, of course, shocked. I believe from the beginning when I started in the UN mission that the -- as the UN to be the highest authority. And I did my best in the whole mission and I was later on serving in Kashmir for one year, also as an operation officer and also had high postings. I was, of course, shocked when this happened, and I still remember that all the UNMOs we were sure about that now that it was an UNMO observed that it was fired from the BiH side. And a day after the UN spokesman, Gary Coward, I went down to the press conference that he made, he was informing the press that this was -- this incident was done by the Bosnian Serb side, although the UNMOs had reported different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Captain, are you aware that -- did you know who General Meille was at the time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't know that he was the acting sector commander of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: General Meille?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Meille, M-E-I-L-L-E, Frenchman.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 30th of June he sent a letter to the accused in this case, the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, protesting the firing of the air bomb by the Bosnian Serb side that hit the TV tower? In other words, he concluded that it was fired from the Serb side; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever learn on the 30th of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P103, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 30th of June, 1995, the accused in this case, the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at the time, sent a report in which he said that the Bosnian Serb forces had hit the TV building on the 28th of June, 1995? Did you ever hear that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I heard that from one of your assistants when calling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear it at the time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does that information cause you to think that perhaps the UNMO that provided you this information had been mistaken, since the commander of the SRK himself was saying on the 30th of June that they had hit the TV tower?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: When I got the information, when you called me, I believe it was one of your assistants that called me in Denmark, that, of course, caused me to think if there should be anything wrong in the report. But when writing the report, when questioning the UNMO, and at that time, still I -- I believe that what we were writing in the report was fully correct. We were aware that it -- it could have -- as I said earlier, it could have a big impact on the situation if this was known, but still we had all reasons to believe that the report was correct and the UNMO what he saw was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've -- my final question: You have suggested -- you have indicated there was lot of discussion about this in the days that followed about this rumour, about this information that it had been fired from the BiH side. Did you ever learn, hear of anyone else who says that he or she saw it fired from that location?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: You mean this particular one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. Did you ever learn of anyone else who said, Yes, I also saw it fired from that location, or I saw a launcher truck at that location? Did you ever hear of anyone else --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: If I had ever heard anything like that, I would have reported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you report it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear from anyone that they have seen this missile, rocket was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you. One matter. I'm not sure if the original report which we have been talking about, which is 65 ter 536, I don't know if that is in evidence under a different number. If it is not, I think it certainly should be in evidence. The report of the 29th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will ask the court deputy if he can help us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's D103, and we also have the drawing in D103. We have an additional piece of paper which is the drawing made by the UNMO. Now, for the 65 ter list 536, we have an additional piece of paper that is the drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. If it is already in evidence, then there is no need to move it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm finished, but I do have an administrative matter which I have already mentioned to the Defence. D72 is the statement of the witness. For some reasons that version is in evidence is unsigned. We have a signed version and the parties both agree to substitute the signed version for the unsigned version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll arrange with the registrar to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just have a question of a technical nature. Could we increase the temperature in the courtroom because I'm beginning to get very cold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will ask the court deputy to look into that

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness. My name is Branislava Isailovic. I am defending the Dragomir Milosevic, and I'm a lawyer working for the Paris Bar Association. I'm going to put you a few questions regarding some of the matters that were addressed by the Prosecutor this morning. Now, to begin with, I would like to ask you a few questions about the reporting procedure which is established by UNMO and according to certain rules. Could you tell the Chamber, and could you tell us all, what is the purpose of these observation posts, like OP4 that you mentioned? What role do they play?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: The observation post was supposed to report about shelling incidents, movements from troops on both sides, and report what they saw and not what they believed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
