utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, all the observation posts were staffed by several UNMOs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I don't understand the word "staffed."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: There were several people that were members of a team that was at the observation post; is that how things happened?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. The observation post, as it's called here, was not only observation post, it was a team site. From one of the teams, as you could see in the picture, it's on top of one of the mountains, and it was then as well a good observation post to look into the city of Sarajevo, or part of it, and from there to report what they could see. Your question about several UNMOs, in every UNMO team, which this was an UNMO team, there was always several UNMOs in -- in a team that could be in the UN mission in the former Yugoslavia. It could be all from three UNMOs and up to 18, 20 UNMOs in a team. In this particular team, I believe, as I remember, there was six, seven UNMOs, but some of them would then be on leave. That meant that at all times there would be five, six UNMOs. Some could then be on patrol. They could be somewhere else. I believe that at all times, because it was a good observation post as well, there would always be at least be two UNMOs present at the team site.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, the other members, with the exception of these two UNMOs that remained at all times on the observation post, were part of the teams that were conducting the investigations in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: It's correct that the UNMOs they were taking or carrying out investigation, or it could also be liaison to the parts. When the team was placed on the BiH side, then liaison would be the BiH; or if it is a team on the Bosnian Serb side, then it would be liaison to that side. They were to carry out investigation, observations as well, in the way that they were to observe if there were any troop movements, if the confrontation line was moving - the cease-fire line, was the correct name - if there were any movements in that one, there could be reports from either the Bosnian Serb side or the BiH side. But now the other part had moved the confrontation line, or they had on this line that was agreed to keep this line, that one of the parts had gone on further, that they were supposed to be. As far I remember, I believe that there always two observers at the team site because it was a good place for observation. But you must not understand me the way that -- that I'm 100 per cent sure that there was always two UNMOs present at the team site. And as I'm writing in the report, it's -- we took contact -- I have all reason to believe that we took contact to the UNMOs present at the team site. And as I have reported, they were taking shelter at the time when the incident happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hansen, I'm asking you these questions -- to begin with, these are questions of a general nature. I would like to know what your job was all about. What was your exact position in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: You mean my own position or the UNMO position?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about you specifically, your job.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: My specific job was to be the operation officer. There was 80 military observers, UN Military Observers in Sector Sarajevo. Above me, there was the -- the sector chief for the UNMOs and there was a deputy, and then I was the operation officer. I was -- I was the one to -- to make the planning for who was to make which investigations, or the overall planning for the UNMOs; and then in the team, there would be a team leader that then would delegate the -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the name of your superior at the UNMO headquarters in Sarajevo, please? Was it perhaps Major Sundquest?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No. He was the deputy for the -- for the UNMO for the whole of Bosnia. There was -- the organisation of the UNMOs was that there was a headquarters for the overall former Yugoslavia and that headquarters was placed in Zagreb; then there was -- there was the headquarters for the UNMOs in overall Bosnia, and that was Major Sundquest. He was the deputy in command of the overall for Bosnia; and then in Bosnia, you have different sectors, and one of the sectors was Sarajevo. The only thing is that Major Sundquest, he was then -- the overall headquarters for Bosnian was placed in Sarajevo as well, but we were two different headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And what about you? You were part of the Sarajevo headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Was your superior Tarik Alam [phoen] perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember at the time. I know that -- if you mean -- in report here, I can see that Colonel Alam was the DSMO. He was the deputy sector military observer. And so I believe at the time of the report, the SMO, the sector military observer, he was not present, the senior -- he was not present, so the Lieutenant-Colonel Alam, as far as I remember, he was from Bangladesh. He was working as the sector senior and my superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, how did the reporting procedure work? Now, to conduct investigations, you always used the reports which were filed by the UNMOs, and these were sent to the headquarters in Sarajevo and then the Sarajevo headquarters reported back to Zagreb. Is that how the reporting procedure worked?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, for instance, people that were posted at OP4 Vikovac, we mentioned this observation post, now, according to the regular procedure, did things happen this way? In the event that somebody saw something, the people there drafted a report or called you up via radio, and they called you up in the headquarters in Sarajevo; is that how things worked?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: It worked the way if it was normal observations. If it was incoming or outgoing shells, they would just report by radio. That was the normal way of reporting it, if they saw something. It was only when they made investigations they made a report, a written report which they brought into -- to my office; and then from that report, we would report further on to headquarters Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned incoming and outgoing shots, who wrote down what was heard on the radio? Was this written down somewhere at the headquarters and at the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: At the operation office, we had four operation officers that was monitoring the radio at all times from the UNMO, and they writing down the report. So by the end of the day, we had a full report of what was happening in the sector, and that was the report that I was then to finalise and send to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So your report, let's call it your final report, the one which was drafted at the end of the day, was this a half daily report or a daily report which was sent off to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That was a report by the end of the day, it was to be sent at 1800 hours and then we continued. It was 24 hours duty at the OP room; and by 2400 hours, we sent the final report for the day or the update of the report. Most of the things they had until 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, there was just a single report that described everything that had happened during the day, the previous day, and the report focussed on everything that had occurred from the day before at 1800 hours until the day when it was sent at 1200 hours?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No. The report that was sent at 1800 hours reported about things that happened from 000 hours, from midnight, until 1800 hours, and then a update of a report was sent by midnight from what happened from 1800 hours to 2400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you always had two reports which bore the same date; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, anything that had been reported over the radio was -- had been written down somewhere by these operators that were operating in the OP room 24 hours a day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, you drafted your report on the basis of the information or the data that had been written down over a particular period by these operators; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. They were writing it down immediately, and they started that there was a continuously report going on. So it meant by the end of the day, by 1800 hours, as operation officer, I only had to finalise this report. They had started on it. So what they were reporting was, for example, the incoming shell, they were counting that now there had been -- from this grid reference there had been outgoing shells, and some other UNMOs they could then report that approximately the tame time there had been incoming -- incoming rounds. And that was reported by the operation officers that was taking care of the radio room. They were putting that into a report that had to be finalised by me at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hansen, what relationship was there between UNMO and UNPROFOR at the time, I mean the UNPROFOR battalions? What kind of reporting procedures was between the two?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: The relation was extremely good in the way that the -- the Sector Sarajevo for the UNPROFOR, the headquarter was -- or the operation room was next to the operation room from the UNMOs. So it meant that whenever things happened we went to the office from each other so we could inform what was going on, and they also received the report that I filed. And I was -- when I was present at the PTT building, I was always present when the -- when there was an operation report from the Sector Sarajevo UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of relationship did you have to the local police. I'm going to ask you a number of questions here. We addressed a report introduced by the Prosecutor relating to the incident that occurred on the 28th of June. You were shown -- I don't have if you have this before you, but we can show it to you. This is Exhibit P134. Do you remember ever having written a -- or mentioned or looked into a report which had been drafted by the Bosnian police?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember to have seen that before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you would agree that the Bosnian police says that you took part, or rather, you were present when the investigation took place. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I agree that I was present at the -- at the-- the scene, at the TV building, but I was not present when any investigation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, you knew nothing about it. They did it on their own bat and didn't keep you informed about anything; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No. It's not correct in that way. It happened sometimes that we carried out the investigations from the UNMO, and from the BiH that they were carried out at the same time. But very often it could happen that it -- that we arrived to the scene maybe later than the BiH and, therefore, we didn't do the investigations together. And I didn't expect to do the investigation in this case, together with the BiH because that would not be normal, but because it would be two different investigation teams. The UNMO's report would never rely on the observations from the BiH investigation team and the other way around. The BiH would not agree on -- or agree is not the correct word. But every team was doing their own investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: My question was somewhat different, but you did provide an answer. Now, let's get back here to this particular report where your name has been mentioned, Captain Thomas. Was this you, Captain Idriz? These are your first names, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: This is my first name, and that's because it is common in Denmark that we use the first name. For some of the other observers, it could be the last name, the family name, but I don't know. For sure it is me that is being referred to in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: How did they know your name? The policeman who was writing this report, did you introduce yourself? Had you worked together perhaps beforehand? How did he get to know your name?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: When arriving to a crime scene, when the BiH was present, we would always request who was present at the time. So that was normal procedure from the BiH side that they would have the names of the people present. And as I informed the Court about earlier, I was present there for, I believe, two hours, but was not allowed to carry out any investigation, so that can be the reason why they include my name in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And all these people, there are 12 people in total, did they introduce themselves to you, these policemen?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you knew that these were policemen, did you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: When, as I informed earlier - informed earlier, when I came to the crime scene, we went to the place where there was damages from the bomb. We were then taken to what they meant to be a secure place, and that was the reason for them to keep us away from the scene. I believe for sure I would have been introduced to maybe one or two of those people that were present, but we didn't see -- or I myself didn't see the investigation team from the BiH side. But for sure they would have been carrying out an investigation. So I believe the reason for me being in the report and all of the other names that was the normal procedure from the BiH side. I don't find anything strange in -- in the way that have been doing, except I was not present during their investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you did not co-sign this report, did you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hansen, I would like to address the issue of the relationship between UNMO, you yourself, and the other UNMOs and the ABiH army. So there were liaison officers who were in the same building as you; in other words, the PTT building. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And there is was this captain of the -- Nermin Silajdzic, captain of the ABiH army; do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Also Captain Goro?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: There were several of them. There were several liaison officers; is that right? Which of these officers threatened you on the 28th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a threat, but it was Captain Nermin that wanted me to leave the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You weren't armed, were you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But Captain Nermin was, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No. I don't remember the liaison officer to be armed, but probably they were armed. But as a military observer, you are not armed and I don't remember him as being armed or not being armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached the site where an incident had occurred, you were not armed and you were there together with local police. Were there other soldiers of the ABiH army, for instance, who came to those sites where you were conducting your investigations?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: If I remember, there were soldiers. But as the situation in Sarajevo at that time was really tense and it was -- the real war going on at that moment, so for sure there had been some soldiers around.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hansen, you were somebody doing your job in the midst of a war, and you were doing injure job at the time when there was a lot of armed people around you. What were your feelings about this? You were doing your job. How did you feel about feeling secure and area job and not being armed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: To be honest, I find it a little bit irrelevant, but that is because all the UNMOs are unarmed. And the reason for that is that if we carry a pistol or a gun or anything, that would not secure us in being in those situations. By being unarmed, both parties, the BiH and Bosnian Serbs, then you and everyone knew that the UNMOs were unarmed. So if anything should happen to us, to be armed would never help us. So I didn't feel unsecure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But members of UNPROFOR, FreBat, and the other battalions, for instance, were armed and quite heavily armed, if one can say so?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever together with UNPROFOR soldiers, were you ever together with the Bosnian police on the same investigation site with UNPROFOR people?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That is two questions. Of course, we were together with the UNPROFOR soldiers, as we were in the same building and I was taking part in -- in reporting together with the UNPROFOR soldiers and the battalions. Second question about it, if I was ever together with Bosnian police on the same investigation side, with UNPROFOR people, there might be UNPROFOR soldiers present at a scene, but that was not likely. Normally, the UNPROFOR troops didn't have any -- anything to do with investigations. Investigations was always carried out by UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But have you heard about the FreBat who was investigating sniping incidents or shelling?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: When you called it "investigating," it was not investigating in the way that the UNMOs were supposed to investigate. When the FreBat or any of the other battalions, because it was other battalions than the FreBat present in the Sector Sarajevo, they were carrying out the investigations in order to -- to stop, for example, the sniping. We were only supposed to make the investigations to report about it, to have it as an evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you have a document in front of you. I don't know how to identify it. It's -- it starts with "Confidential," and it's about the incident that occurred between the liaison officer and Captain Hansen. It is something that was given to you by the Prosecutor. Do you see this document? It's got several pages. I believe everyone has it, but maybe we could call it. It's document P519. A number of questions were asked to you by the Prosecutor, as well as by the learned Judges. So I looked into the structure of this report. This is a report that has several appendixes. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So the report was written on July 5, 1995, sent to your HQ in Zagreb, to give information on this incident, but not on the air bomb that had been -- that would have been launched, but on the incident that occurred after this bomb was launched. Right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor underlined one thing, and I would like to repeat it. On page 4 of this bundle, it is said the following: "Patrol report," and this is the not the report on the bomb itself. The liaison officer, Mr. Nermin Silajdzic, reported the incident he had with you to his senior officer, I guess, the incident that occurred on June 28th in the evening. And you also wrote everything that happened during this encounter with this liaison officer; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And there is another report, let's call it the normal report, that had been sent at 1800 hours, dated June 28, where there the incident regarding the bomb is reported to your HQ in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So already at that moment you had the information you got from Captain Idriz from Kenya. He is the one who actually saw the bomb being launched, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent that he was the one, but I was from that site. I was given a list of UNMOs present at the -- in the sector at the moment; and by looking at the names, Captain Idriz was the name that came up in my mind as being the one that had seen this rocket or whatever it was that was launched. As I informed -- I'm sure that this UNMO was one present on the BiH side. He was from religion. He was Muslim and that was one of the things that he was mentioning at the first when he came to my office, that even though he was a Muslim himself, he had to report because he believe in the UN and only reporting on what you see. And, you know, even though he was a Muslim, he then had to file this report or to inform me about what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, to your opinion, and it may be just an assumption on my side, but when you saw Captain Nermin Silajdzic, and I read in your report on page 4 of this document, where you actually giving report on the actual timing of what you did, and then there is a very long paragraph in this report where you say: "[In English] At that time there was a reported more than 50 outgoing rounds from heavy weapons outside the PTT building." [Interpretation] And then you continue saying that you walked into Captain Nermin Silajdzic's office. So this was quite a long period of time since then, of course. But do you think that he knew from seeing you that you had guessed what the truth was? That you had guessed that the bomb had come from the BiH side, that you hat found that out?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I'm not sure how he would be able to know that of the.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I uphold that. He can't answer that, but ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to get his feeling because a great number of questions of like this were asked of this witness, and this is why I ask this question because when you read the report something actually happened, obviously. Something quite striking, bizarre, I don't know what you want to call it. And I'm asking the witness whether he remembers a different reaction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you can ask him about the reaction of the person. You can ask him about how he reacted, but he can only testify as to what he knows or what he sees.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this person's reaction, when you walked into his office, was it bizarre compared to the reactions he usually had on other days? Did he react differently?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I don't think he reacted different in comparison with other days where the fighting was going on like it was on that day. When there is fighting going on, people are stressed; myself, I believe, as well. And the reason for his reaction is probably, as I mentioned earlier, that when I asked him to stop fire, that was a common thing for us to do as military observers. That when there were casualties, when there were incidents where it could have an a reason to ask the both parties to stop firing for half an hour or something for medical treatment to get in and out, that was common for to us go down and ask for. When I asked him to stop firing, as a I mentioned in my report, he said, What firing? And the BiH they had just outside the PTT building, they had weapons and everyone of us could hear and see from the building that they were firing towards the Bosnian Serb side. That was natural because the fighting was going on from both sides, but his reaction was that he said to me, What fire? Then when I told him there was these weapons placed outside, this misunderstanding, I believe, came up where he asked me, Do you believe that we have fired against ourselves. When I was questioning about the PTT -- no, sorry. When I questioned about stopping the fire because of the incident at the TV building, my answer to him was that we had no reason to believe where the fire came from. When we had carried out the investigation, I would tell him where we believed the fire would have come from. And that is the part where I believe that maybe between the lines understood. Because I must be honest to say as well that by knowing this report from the UNMO, I maybe have difficulties to express myself or to -- to show impartiality, if that is the correct word.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to your report and not the report that was given by the Prosecutor, but document D103, because that is the one that has the additional sketch attached it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please call that up on the screen, so it's D103 plus the drawing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I see that you have that drawing in hand, do you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So let's be very clear: This drawing was made by the person that might be Captain Idriz. That's 90 per cent sure that it might be Captain Idriz. And this was the person that saw the projectile launched and impacting the roof of the TV building.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: One last question. You already explained, but this is for the transcript. You said that normally in reports you report on behalf of an UNMO but you don't give the name of the person that provided the information that helped draft the daily report.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. That when we sent this report or in the report we sent for -- for the UNMO headquarters in Zagreb there would only be the name on the reporting officer from our headquarter and not from the UNMO that had been doing the observation or investigation, because that would be filed somewhere else, if there would be a written report about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain. I have just a few final questions. One question relates to the kind of fire that you heard outside the PTT building when you were speaking to the BiH liaison officer. Was that just ordinary rifle fire or was it machine-guns or any major weaponry involved in that exchange of fire from the BiH side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was all kind of weapons at that time, including mortar and firing of grenades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Tell me, if you can, how close to the PTT building did the BiH employ heavy weaponry, like mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within 100 metres at times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you had seen this occurring frequently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question, or my last question to you, relates to the information given to you by this UNMO, and I would like the registrar to bring us back the picture taken from the top of the building? I believe it was Exhibit number P518. And also if we could have split up on the screen at the same time the previous Exhibit number P517 which was map with the spots. Could we have those brought up together? And while we are waiting for the pictures to come up, Captain, my question to you relates to what you could have seen from the parking place below the terrace where we are now on the picture to your left. I understand that the place where the car was parked was underneath this parking place shown on the picture. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the direction from the grid reference to the TV building, if the fire came from behind that industrial building that we see in the yellow frame, the direction of the fire would then have been -- that the fire would have been shot somewhere behind that building and then had had its trajectory towards the right, if I compare this with the map next to it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you remember what you could actually see when you were standing on the lower parking place at the time? You told us, when I asked you this question before, that he showed you the place from which you -- from which he said the shot had been fired. But what could you actually see from down there? Can you be very precise and tell me, could you see, for instance, the ground? Was it possible to see from the level below this the actual ground from where the launcher might have stood, or was behind of industrial building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could remember, you could see into ground on some places between the buildings. And I said earlier, the new building with grey, blue, red was not built at the time, as far as I remember. So it was -- for me, it was good reasons to believe that he could -- as he reported, that he could see the projectile all the way from where it was fired and to the impact on the building. I had no reason not to believe that this could not have happened, that he had seen that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No. But you could see with your own eyes the ground, and you would have a clear view towards the east from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. To the TV building, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Captain --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm a little concerned about one thing on where there have been a misunderstanding in terms of where the lower parking lot is located in the relation to the upper parking lot, just based on our own observations. And I don't know -- I'm not sure it ultimately has import, but I'm a little concerned about the record being left with what may be a misunderstanding based on the witness's understanding of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I suggest we ask the witness about it, but my -- the reason why I'm asking this, of course, is that from the upper platform, where we were, you would have a very good view. And my recollection was when we were at the site that if you would have gone down, you would have been able to see less. So this is why I'm asking the captain what could he actually see, because depending on where exactly the car was parked underneath, he might have had a good view. And I understand the witness as saying that, yes, he did have a quite good view from downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't dispute that, and I think the evidence is clear on that. It's just that I think that the lower parking lot is not underneath the upper parking lot; it's next to it but lower. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That could well be, but the answer offered by the witness is the important thing; namely, that he was able to see the ground and the possible trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I was part of the visit. So it's not next to it, but I believe this -- it's in the prolongation. It's an extension of this little wall. That's where we could have the parking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why don't you put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, please, could you look at the picture again, the picture that is on the screen. According to your recollection, could you tell us what was the position of what you called the upper parking and the lower parking lot on this photograph. Could you tell us where the upper parking lot would be and the lower parking lot would be?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: I find it difficult from this picture to -- to recall the scene. But as far as I remember from standing at his car where we went down to, there is a lower parking place, lower than this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you, Captain, at the time of this incident how old were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to calculate. I'm born in 1962, so I must have been 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thirty-three. And how many years service in the army had you had at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only had two years of services in the Danish army at that time. I was an officer of the reserve and the infantry. And in the Danish army, we have the tradition that we have an officer of the reserve and then you have to serve a certain number of days, weeks, months every year. So you are called in and retrained, and you can only graduate in rank by going through different courses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask you: How long were you in the company of the UNMO officer who made the report to you on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't fully understand your question. If you mean how long I have been in the mission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I'm talking about the UNMO officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it Captain Idriz? You're 90 per cent that it is Captain Idriz? He made the report to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And was he in your company for some time after that; and if so, for how long? How long did you see him on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it was Captain Idriz I, can see from the report that he went to the PTT building together with me, so he had probably been together with me for three, four hours that day. But it was not common for to us be four hours together with the UNMOs being in the teams, and I'm being present at the operation rooming. I was visiting the teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So he was with you for about three, four hours. During that time did you speak with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And were you able to form an impression of his character, of his intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the whole period serving together in Sector Sarajevo, together with him, I have no reason not to -- to see him as a proper and good working UNMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you had in fact known him before then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But, sir, not personally in any way, because with -- I came from another sector, Sector East, where have I been serving for six months. And at the time of this incident, I have been in Sector Sarajevo for, I believe, five months. And with 80 observers and at the time of situation was tense, we didn't have near -- we didn't know each other personally, only a few of the observers knew. Because myself working in the PTT building as an operation officer, that was 16, 18 hours a day and by reporting and going around and doing investigations. So you don't have that personal contact to many of the UNMOs. That is probably the reason why I don't recall his name because he was not one that I had -- had any reason to -- to pay more attention to than other UNMOs before this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He was a captain, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If he was the one, he was a captain. But I recall him as a young UNMO. When I recall the picture, when he came into the office, I recall him as a young officer; and by "young" that means probably captain. And by going through the list of the UNMOs present at the time in Sector Sarajevo, excluding people being on the Bosnian Serb side, being in the teams and so on, I believe this is the UNMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were 33 at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would he have been younger than that age, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is difficult to see on people when coming from different nationalities and so on. I believe he was of my age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of the knowledge that you had of him, in particular the three or four hours that he was in your company on that day, would you have any reason to believe that he was confused in giving this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain, I have one last question for you. When I look at your report of June 28, you write about two UNMOs. The first one says that the projectile left from grid BP 866587 on BiH territory; and the second UNMO says that the projectile, which looks more like a rocket, was launched from the north-west. So according to you, is it the same direction, or did the observers make a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where do we say that it says he reports seeing it coming from the west?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the second page, third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, I see it. When the UNMO has been reporting, so I have been writing it in my report and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But my question is you, as their -- the officer in charge of operations, do you think that these two reports converge or diverge? At your level, you heard those two people, did you think what they were saying corresponded or did not match.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure I had been thinking about it at that time, but you must know that at the time the fighting was going on from both sides. So there was not only this one projectile in the air at this time. There could have been others. If you want me to answer your question, if I think there is something strange or different in the way that they are reporting, I need time to think about it, because I -- I know that when reporting that at the time when filing the report, this is what I believed and this is what the UNMOs they informed me. And they way of reporting, as an UNMO, we were not to make any conclusions in our report. We were only to report what the UNMOs that came in reported to us, although it might be of different -- I mean, that it wouldn't draw one conclusion. We were only to send the report and then it was for other people, like you now, to make conclusions if this is an important or not. So at the time I reported this because this is what the UNMO informed me; and by looking at it right now, I can't conclude myself if this is a different thing that they are reporting or if it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Captain, do you remember when I asked you about the superior officer from Zagreb who told you to forget about the report of this incident? You indicated that he called a second time and he told you, I believe, that the matter had been settled. Did he say anything else? What is your understanding as to what he meant by the matter had been settled? Did he provide any further information on what had happened to settle the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no opinion about why he was calling me, only that when I have reported this I was not supposed to take any other matters on the affair. There's also one thing that I also mentioned for -- I don't remember your name on that side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Prosecutor is enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I mentioned when they called me or one assistant called me was that I was asked about the grid reference that we reported in the report. This report went, as I said earlier, to the headquarter for the whole sector for the whole of Bosnia, and they were carrying out an investigation. They sent some special troops. I believe it was SAS people to the grid reference. Later on that afternoon or the day after, they told me that because we had near contact, a good cooperation sometimes where we could not carry out an investigation, they could have possibilities to look into the areas. And they told me that they had been on the grid reference and carried out investigation, and there was -- they couldn't find any evidence of anything fired from the place. But from the grid reference where they have been was not the same that we had given in the report, so there must have been a misunderstanding somewhere, because they had not been on this place where the grid reference is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How narrow is a grid point? Is it ten square metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This grid given here is within 100 metres. So it's for -- for you, sirs, the first two numbers is the grid reference. If you have a grid on the map, then it's one square kilometre, a square kilometer. And for the certain number in the grid reference is 100 metres, then you can give a fourth one and it would be within ten metres. So the UNMO gave a grid reference; and from where he pointed out we gave reference with 100 metre. But the grid reference, as far as I recall it, it was SAS troops that had been sent to the grid reference. They didn't refer to the same grid reference. I think that was 5, 600 metres from the grid reference we have given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But tell me one thing: The grid reference we see on the map, 866587, is that one kilometre on each side, one square kilometre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is one square kilometre. I believe that is one kilometre. It's normal that you have one kilometre in the grids.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But can you recall, looking at the map, what is the distance between the PTT building and the grid reference, the red spot on the map, and the TV building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's 4, 500 metres as I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: From which point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the PTT building, it is around 4, 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And to the TV building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the grid reference to the TV building, it will be around 7, 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the grid reference, the red spot, what does that actually signify? Because if the grid reference refers to an area which is one kilometre by one kilometre --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sorry. The grid reference refers to a square 100 metre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You mean the one shown on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay, well, then I understand better okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one question arising out of Judge Mindua' questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have Exhibit 518 on the screen, if we could focus on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, Captain Hansen, I am going to go back to the notation of the 29th of June in your report in which Judge Mindua asked you about, in which you say that another UNMO, who was in the parking lot at the PTT, believed the sound of the rocket was from the north-west. Now, just looking at the map here, the grid reference that you have identified in your report is to the north, north-east of the PTT building, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if the UNMO believed that the sound came from the north-west, from the PTT building, then that would be something different from it being launched from the grid reference that have you identified. That would be a different place?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That would be a different place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: But my report also says that he looked, and I only reported what he told me. He looked in the direction where he heard or believed to have heard something, and he didn't see anything. There is a lot of buildings, so there would be echo from the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the -- according to the report, he looked after the sound of the impact, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it's not surprising that if he looked -- after the bomb landed, if looked towards the direction where he heard it was coming from, he would not see anything. That's not surprising, is it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Question, one last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Hansen, it seems when you look at the second part of your report, it seems that this person thought that he had heard the sound and then looked in that direction the sound came from and saw nothing. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS HANSEN
utterances.text: That's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Captain Hansen, that concludes your testimony. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take a relatively extended break to allow for the voice distortion and the other technical facilities to be set up for the next witness. We're adjourned until quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hereby declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sachdeva, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I just want to check that you can hear me in a language that you understand and that you can also see me. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Yes, I can understand and I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I also want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, perhaps I should have clarified at the outset, for the benefit of the record, that this witness is giving evidence by video conference link. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I also want to confirm to you, Witness, that the Court has granted you protective measures and therefore I will be referring to you as Witness 95, and you should take care not to say anything that would identify you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go into private session so I can elicit the personal details, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness 95, do you remember giving a statement to persons from the Tribunal on the 8th of July, 2006? That is, last year.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you remember that the statement you gave referred to an incident in Bunicki Potok, on the 1st of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, did members of the Tribunal visit your house yesterday, that is Sunday, and read through the statement that you gave in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And after they read through the statement, are you now able to confirm that what is contained in that statement is accurate and true, to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Everything is correct. There are no mistakes at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that 65 ter 03065 be shown to the witness and also brought up on e-court, and that it's not broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness W-95, you will be shown a statement in a moment by the court officer down there in Sarajevo. If you can just confirm for me when have you that in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. I actually -- it's actually 03067, the ter number. Excuse me for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness W-95, do you have that statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the first page, if you could look at the bottom of the first page, do you see your thumb print there on that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: I see it there, yes. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that that statement be enter into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes P520 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness W-95, I have just one question for you, so I'm not going to take too much of your time. But on that incident on the 1st of July in 1995, were you injured by the shell that landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Yes, I was. It was not a shell; it was something larger than a shell. It was like an air bomb. It was not a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what happened to you? What injuries did you sustain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: I sustained injuries in my left shoulder. I have two pieces of shrapnel, which they couldn't take out, and they're still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you as a result of those injuries have to -- were you admitted to hospital as a result of those injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Yes, I was. They took me to hospital right away. I was in the hospital until 2.00. They tried and tried to take it out and they couldn't. There were many wounded in the hospital. It was overcrowded. They spent me back home. So I was at home and I would drift in and out of consciousness. They took me to a private clinic. The doctor helped me, then they took me to the month military hospital to get an X-ray. I couldn't get up. I would try to raise my head, and then I would begin to lose consciousness; and then they took my back home, and ten days later I went again for them try and take the pieces of shrapnel out. And the doctor said it's not worth slitting the throat of an ox just to get two kilograms of meat out of it. They said if we were to take out these pieces of shrapnel, we would have to amputate your arm. There's no other way to do. And so to this very day I'm having problems all over my left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness W-95, thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Isailovic. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'm Branislava Isailovic. I'm a lawyer with the Paris Bar, and I defend the accused in these proceedings, General Dragomir Milosevic. I'm going to ask you a few questions regarding your statement which you just dealt with the Prosecutor. First question: You did not sign this signature with your handwriting, is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: No. I'm illiterate. I did put my thumb print there. It's the same as a signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like my case manager to call up a document that should not be broadcast. 65 ter document 3068.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And could the court officer in Sarajevo show this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Yes, I made that statement. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, this is your statement dated October 7, 1995. Could you please look at the end of the statement. You -- there is your signature at the very bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: There is a signature there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: They came and they put questions to me. I couldn't sign and then maybe somebody else signed, but I was not aware. I was not conscious. I'm not literate. Somebody else might have signed. I'm not afraid of anything. I will only speak the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, maybe you remember who signed in your place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: I don't know. I have nothing to do with it. I was not myself. I was in the hospital. The hospital staff could have signed. There were foreign organisations there asking questions. I was not myself. Who signed this? Well, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on October 7, 1995, you were still in the hospital after your injury? This was a few months later, and there statement is dated October 7, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in the hospital. I wasn't in hospital. But I was always seeing doctors, and I'm still under medical supervision to this day. I was under the supervision of doctors a lot, and I still am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But my question is the following: You made the statement that we have just seen, and it was a statement that you made in front of police officers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: There is the signature of a policeman. So could you tell us if a policeman was actually there to take your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was a long time ago, 12 years ago. I don't remember who was there, let me tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, you say that you were in the apartment or the house of your daughter-in-law -- somebody from the family. So you were not in your own house at the time. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: We were expelled from our house. We arrived there as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you were in the house of this relative because you were a refugee.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: She was not my daughter-in-law but my sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And at the time did you know Hrasnica well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I did because it wasn't far from my village.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's at the foot of Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Witness. I was asked to repeat my question. But the witness did answer my question. So for the transcript, this was my question. Was it close to Mount Igman; and then in line 11 the witness answered my question. This wasn't intended for you. This was a mere technical issue. The question I'd like to put to you now runs as follows: At the time, did you know about Igman road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: No. The road -- I knew the road. I knew some roads and pathways but not those.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In Hrasnica, at that time, were there a lot of soldiers passing through the village, soldiers on their way to Mount Igman? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: There were no soldiers there at all. There were only civilians there. There was nothing military there at all. There were only civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And precisely what is a civilian person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: A civilian, for example, are women, elderly men, children. That's what I call civilians. People who were not carrying a rifle were civilians. People who were not able to carry a rifle were civilians in my view.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So in Hrasnica, you actually -- during this period when the war was on, you never saw any male carrying any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: I didn't. The soldiers were up there on Mount Igman. People knew where the lines were. The soldiers didn't come down to Hrasnica, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know how these people got to Igman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: Who, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-95
utterances.text: The soldiers went up to Igman. The lines were set. They kept the lines, and there was something called UNPROFOR between the lines. The Serbs were there in Trnovo and Vejsici, and our soldiers were up there on Igman. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll wait now for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, we don't have another witness for today. We tried as we might to schedule two witnesses for today and we just had difficulties doing it, and we couldn't schedule a second witness for today. This is the only witness for today. I apologise for the loss of time, approximately 25 minutes. We are confident that we can fit the witnesses into the three remaining days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of April, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.20 p.m.,
